US Central Command (Centcom) said the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) launched two one-way attack drones towards Bahrain, both of which were intercepted by US forces.
Centcom also rejected the IRGC’s claim that it had attacked a US early-warning radar in Bahrain earlier in the day.
The competing accounts come amid questions from some US lawmakers about the Pentagon’s disclosure of details surrounding incidents in the conflict, while scepticism has also circulated on social media.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Art against erasure: A Palestinian sculptor and a Lebanese painter on war, exile and memory
data.author: Victoria Brittain
data.summary:
Art against erasure: A Palestinian sculptor and a Lebanese painter on war, exile and memory
Submitted by
Victoria Brittain
on
Fri, 11/13/2026 - 12:11
Abdul Rahman Katanani and Ayman Baalbaki, close as brothers, have spent decades turning the violence of their youth into work shown in museums and collections worldwide
Abdul Rahman Katanani in his studio outside Beirut (Victoria Brittain/MEE)
Off
The large studios of Abdul Rahman Katanani and Ayman Baalbaki are filled with canvases and installations about memory and destruction, drawn from the Israeli wars that shaped both artists’ youth.
These magical spaces, one in an anonymous building in busy central Beirut, and the other far from the city in a village high in the hills, speak for Lebanon and Palestine.
They also define the two artists and their families.
Katanani’s materials are barbed wire, corrugated metal sheets, olive branches, petroleum barrels and discarded clothes from his birthplace, the Sabra and Shatila refugee camp.
“I’ve always wanted to use the materials of the camp. These materials are our shadows. No... they’re us,” he told Middle East Eye.
The harsh materials yield startling lyrical shapes, such as a nine-metre wave in barbed wire, a child playing, a lotus flower and a bright early collage of clothes, including the unexpectedly intimate detail of underwear.
Once, he built a replica of the Palestinian camp of his childhood, shown inside an art gallery.
Ayman Baalbaki in his studio (Victoria Brittain/MEE)
Baalbaki’s very large mixed-media paintings are distinctive. They feature multiple thick layers of paint, often acrylic, in both intense and subtle colours. Many form part of a mesmerising series.
One such series, Destruction and Loss , depicts the ruin of Beirut’s iconic buildings, like his 2015-16 iconic painting of the Barakat Building on the corner of Damascus Road on the Green Line of the 15-year-long civil war.

data.author: Oscar Rickett

United Arab Emirates 'imported at least 591 tonnes of illicit gold into the country in 2024', new report from Swissaid finds
Bars of gold in a shop in the Dubai Gold Souk on 13 April 2026 (Fadel Senna/AFP)
Off
The United Arab Emirates remains the key trading hub for smuggled gold and conflict gold, a new report from Switzerland’s Swissaid foundation has found.
Despite the introduction in 2023 of legislation intended to curb illegal flows, the UAE, which is now the world’s second largest gold trading hub after Switzerland, imported at least 591 tonnes of illicit gold into the country in 2024.
Illicit gold refers to that which was either smuggled to the UAE - most often to the gold markets of Dubai, the second largest Emirate - without being able to be traced, or that comes from countries at war, including Yemen, Sudan and Russia.
The UAE remains by far the main destination for gold linked to armed conflicts in Africa, according to Swissaid. It also continues to be a major destination for gold exports from countries subject to international sanctions.
“The findings of this study are deeply concerning. They show that the United Arab Emirates remains a hub for smuggled and conflict gold,” said Marc Ummel, head of Swissaid’s commodities unit and co-author of the study.
In 2024, the UAE imported at least 174.5 tonnes of gold from Russia (directly and indirectly via Armenia), Yemen and Sudan (directly and indirectly), Swissaid found.
Gold leaving Africa for the UAE (Swissaid)
The entire volume from these three countries can, the organisation said, “be considered as conflict gold”.
Gold and war
The UAE has been directly involved in both the wars in Yemen and Sudan, where it is the patron of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary group widely determined to have committed genocide in different parts of Darfur.

data.author: MEE staff
data.summary:

Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Fri, 11/13/2026 - 14:22
Chabad-Lubavitch Hasidic movement distances itself from Gedalia Axelrod's 'personal opinion'
Rabbi Gedalia Axelrod (YouTube screengrab)
Off
A senior Chabad rabbi has been criticised by his own movement after he said it was permissible to kill Jewish Israeli politicians who worked with Arabs.
Gedalia Axelrod, a senior cleric in the Chabad-Lubavitch Hasidic movement, issued a halakhic ruling earlier this week in which he said that Jewish politicians who form a government backed by Palestinian citizens of Israel were "din rodef", which roughly translates as "law of the pursuer".
Under Jewish religious law, a rodef is someone who poses a threat to another person's life and may be stopped by any means necessary.
The doctrine was previously invoked by Yitzhak Rabin’s assassin, Yigal Amir, to justify the prime minister’s killing in 1995.
Axelrod wrote that collaboration with Arab parties "poses a terrible danger to the people of Israel in the Holy Land and around the world".
Collaboration could either take the form of inviting Arab parties to join a governing coalition, or even relying on their support from outside it.
Swift condemnation
Axelrod's comments were swiftly condemned by the leadership of his religious movement, with Chabad spokesperson Rabbi Shimi Segal clarifying that his statements did not represent the official Chabad position.
“Chabad’s official halachic positions are determined exclusively by the Chabad Rabbinical Court, in accordance with the Rebbe’s instructions,” he said.

data.author: Mee User

Palestinian rights group says Israel barred its director from travelling abroad
Israel barred Shawan Jabarin, the general director of Palestinian human rights group Al-Haq, from travelling to Jordan after stopping him at the Allenby Bridge crossing on Friday, the organisation said.
In a statement, Al-Haq said Israeli forces questioned Jabarin about the purpose of his journey before informing him that he was banned from travelling.
The organisation said the restriction were politically motivated and linked to his human rights advocacy.
Al-Haq said Jabarin had previously faced travel restrictions and threats over his work. It cited a 2022 warning call from Israel’s Shin Bet and said a travel ban imposed in 2006 remained in force for six years before being temporarily lifted in 2012.
The organisation said he had also been prevented from travelling to the Netherlands in 2009 to receive a human rights award.

Nine-month-old Kinan Ahmed Raqiq was found dead by his father as they sheltered in a tent in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis overnight.
Raqiq’s father Ahmed, stood weeping outside Nasser Hospital, as he held his son’s shrouded body.
“I woke up only to see his skin had turned blue so I rushed him to Nasser Hospital, but he had already died from hypothermia and frozen to death,” he told AFP.
“I am in complete shock. I found myself holding my son wrapped in a burial shroud.”
Heavy rains have swept through Gaza, inundating thousands of tents where the majority of the enclave’s population are forced to shelter amid ongoing Israeli restrictions on aid entering the territory.
As temperatures plummeted on Thursday, Israeli attacks across Gaza surged, with health officials putting the total toll of people killed since dawn at 11.

An AFP journalist who was at the scene reported that one of the building's exterior staircases had partially collapsed and that indoors an entire floor was damaged, with broken concrete from collapsed walls mixed with broken medical equipment.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Turkey and Qatar sign mutual defence agreement
data.author: MEE staff
data.summary:
Turkey and Qatar sign mutual defence agreement
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Fri, 11/13/2026 - 15:49
Announcement by Turkish presidency is the latest in a series of defence agreements amongst Middle Eastern and Islamic states
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan pictured with Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani during a welcoming ceremony at the presidential complex in Ankara, 8 August 2024 (Murat Cetin Muhurdar/Turkish presidential press office/AFP)
Off
Turkey and Qatar have signed a mutual defence agreement in Istanbul on Friday, in what is the latest military pact between Ankara and other Muslim states.
The defence agreement was one of five agreed between Turkey and Qatar, as President Recep Tayyip Erdogan hosted the Emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani.
A statement by the Turkish president's office said that Friday's mutual defence agreement with Qatar "would add another dimension to our brotherhood".
Erdogan said Turkey and Qatar’s cooperation in the defence industry would continue to grow, according to the statement.
Turkey and Qatar have had several defence agrements since 2017, including the hosting of Turkish troops in Doha, but the new deal obliged both countries to come to the other's defence.
In August this year, Turkey signed a defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, known as the Mecca Agreement.
Last week, the Turkish parliament passed a law approving the Mecca defence pact early on Friday, completing a crucial stage in the legal process.
The move will allow the deployment of Turkish troops to Saudi Arabia, which is currently at war with Yemen's Houthis.
In October, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said that any deployment to Saudi Arabia would be defensive in nature and that Turkish forces would not operate in Yemen.

data.title: Middle East Eye: UN rights chief demands Houthis return body of staff member who died in custody
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
UN rights chief demands Houthis return body of staff member who died in custody
The UN's human rights chief on Friday demanded the return of the body of a Yemeni staff member who died of unknown causes weeks ago, after more than two years in Houthi custody.
Mohammed al-Shami's family learned of his death on 30 October, more than a month after it happened, and has received no explanation of the cause or circumstances.
Al-Shami had been held by the Houthis since 6 June 2024.
"Our colleague must be laid to rest in a dignified manner, in accordance with the wishes of his family - which was denied contact with him for two years while he was in detention," said Volker Turk, the UN high commissioner for human rights.
In a statement earlier this week, Al-Shami's family said the Houthis had agreed in principle to an investigation.
"Do not allow Mohammed to die twice: once when he was taken from his family and disappeared, and again when the truth about his fate is allowed to disappear from the world," the statement said.
More than 70 UN employees and dozens of humanitarian workers remain in detention in Yemen.
Turk's office said a video circulating this week appeared to show one of them "confessing", and voiced fears that the detainees may be subjected to torture or ill-treatment.

Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen, a leading progressive voice in the US Senate on the Middle East, has announced he will mount a leadership challenge to New York Senator Chuck Schumer, who has led the chamber's Democrats since 2017.
Van Hollen posted about his intent to seek the post late on Wednesday night, local time, in Washington, DC.
"In this election, Americans called on us to unrig an economy rigged against working people & fueled by political corruption. To deliver, we need new leadership. This isn't about any one person – it’s about answering that call," he wrote on X.
"That's why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader."
After a stunning midterm election outcome on 3 November that flipped both houses in Congress from red to blue, thanks to progressive messaging and candidates among Democrats, most of the freshman class is seeking a change in leadership.
Key among them is Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who first floated Van Hollen's name as an alternative to Schumer, even though Van Hollen had not given any indication he was interested.
Van Hollen, 67, was elected the same year Schumer became leader.
Schumer, 75, has been largely credited with his fundraising prowess, which enabled Democrats to flip states that haven't seen anyone but a Republican in charge in decades.

data.title: Middle East Eye: France calls for more pressure on Houthis to end attacks on Saudi Arabia
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
France calls for more pressure on Houthis to end attacks on Saudi Arabia
France called for greater pressure on Yemen's Houthis to end their attacks in the region, particularly against Saudi Arabia.
"Our position is that it is necessary to increase pressure on the Houthis so that they put an end to their unacceptable attacks and provocations, particularly against Saudi territory, but not only there," spokesperson for the French foreign ministry Pascal Confavreux told a news conference on Friday.
He was responding to a question on whether Paris backed the idea of the European Union designating the Houthis as a terrorist organisation.
Saudi Arabia is pressing the EU to make the designation, but has yet to overcome European concerns that it could undermine a future peace process, Reuters reported, citing six European officials.
Also on Thursday, the UN Security Council voted unanimously to extend Yemen-related sanctions, including asset freezes and travel bans, for another year, while demanding an end to the group's attacks on Saudi Arabia.
The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) welcomed the resolution on Friday.
"This resolution represents a significant step in consolidating the international stance that rejects the treacherous Houthi attacks," GCC Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi said in a statement.

Lebanese army says it seized arms depot in Beirut's southern suburbs
The Lebanese army said on Friday it had raided an arms depot in Beirut's southern suburbs and arrested one person.
The army carried out "a special security operation after close monitoring of the transportation and trade of weapons", targeting an "arms depot in the Msharrafieh area of the southern suburbs", it said in a statement.
It said troops seized a "large number of war arms and munitions", and that the person arrested is under investigation.
The statement did not say who the weapons belonged to.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Trump says Saudi Arabia is 'disintegrating'
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Trump says Saudi Arabia is 'disintegrating'
Saudi Arabia is “disintegrating”, US President Donald Trump said in an interview released on Friday, which is likely to offend the kingdom, as it suffers missile and drone strikes from Yemen’s Houthis.
Trump passed judgment on Saudi Arabia, one of the US’s closest allies, in an interview with Stephen A Smith, boasting he could destroy Iran in three days by attacking civilian infrastructure but that Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states have asked him not to because of their own weaknesses.
“If I want to take them out, I hit their [energy] in one day. Their energy is gone. In one day, their bridges are gone, and in one day, their manufacturing capability is gone. It would only take me three days, one day each,” Trump said.
"Saudi Arabia has asked me to please just let it be the way it is now for a while because they're disintegrating," Trump said.
"Qatar, if you look at that, Kuwait, UAE, Bahrain, all of them would much prefer the waiting period,” he added.
This is not the first time Trump has appeared to enjoy bragging about the leverage he has over Gulf states and, particularly, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Saudi Arabia has relied on the US as its security guarantor since WWII.
“He (MBS) didn’t think this was going to happen… he didn’t think he’d be kissing my ass… he thought it’d be just another American president that was a loser… but now he has to be nice to me,” Trump said in March, when the war on Iran was in full swing.

If extradited and convicted on the lead charge of international money laundering, Chambers faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison.
